solution.concept_anchor: Tipu Sultan's economic and diplomatic innovations — correct attribution
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because Hyder Ali did introduce French-trained infantry — the error is attributing the 'French alliance embassy of 1787' to him. The 1787 embassy was Tipu's initiative, not Hyder Ali's.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Hyder Ali did introduce French-trained infantry, but the diplomatic embassy to France in 1787 was Tipu Sultan's initiative — Hyder Ali died in 1781, six years before the embassy. The pair conflates two real facts but attributes them to the wrong ruler.

Eliminate (c): Tipu Sultan's economic policies did include state monopolies, but the specific commodity 'indigo' is not historically documented as a Mysorean monopoly — sandalwood, pepper, and cardamom are the correct commodities. Indigo is associated with Bengal plantations.
Eliminate (d): Peshwa Madhav Rao I defeated Hyder Ali in the 1760s, not Tipu Sultan. Tipu faced Maratha power in a different context.
Select (b): Tipu Sultan established state trading monopolies in sandalwood, pepper, and cardamom — this is correctly paired with Tipu's economic administration.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the precision trap: it combines two real facts — Hyder Ali introduced French-trained infantry (true) and the 1787 diplomatic embassy to France (true, but attributed to Tipu, who sent it after succeeding Hyder Ali in 1782). The conflation of these two events under Hyder Ali's name is the trap. Hyder Ali died December 1781; the 1787 embassy could not have been his initiative. A candidate who knows both facts but not their precise temporal attribution will accept option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Precise attribution of policies and events to the correct ruler — Hyder Ali vs. Tipu Sultan — is a standard UPSC precision test.

• Option (a): Incorrectly paired. Hyder Ali did introduce French-trained infantry (true), but the diplomatic embassy to France in 1787 was Tipu Sultan's initiative — Hyder Ali had died in December 1781, six years before the embassy.
• Option (b): Correctly paired. Tipu Sultan established state-controlled trading monopolies in sandalwood, pepper, and cardamom — a documented feature of his economic administration and a direct challenge to EIC commercial interests.
• Option (c): Incorrectly paired. Tipu's state monopolies did not include indigo — that is a Bengal plantation product associated with British economic exploitation in eastern India, not Mysorean state commerce. The correct commodities are sandalwood, pepper, and cardamom.
• Option (d): Incorrectly paired. Peshwa Madhav Rao I defeated Hyder Ali (not Tipu Sultan) in the 1760s. Tipu did face Maratha pressures but the defeat referenced here belongs to Hyder Ali's era.

Value Addition:
• Tipu's economic model — state monopolies replacing private trade — has been compared to mercantilist state capitalism.
• Hyder Ali's French-drilled infantry gave Mysore a decisive advantage in the First War's early battles.
• The correct commodities of Tipu's monopolies (sandalwood, pepper, cardamom) are mnemonic: 'SPC — South's Precious Cargo.'

solution.concept_anchor: Progressive power shift across four Anglo-Mysore Wars

statement_analysis.statement: The shift from Mysore's military effectiveness in the First and Second Wars to British dominance in the Third and Fourth Wars reflects not merely battlefield superiority but also the British capacity to construct and maintain multi-power coalitions against Mysore.
statement_analysis.reason: The British lost or stalemated in wars where their coalitions collapsed (First War — Nizam defected; Second War — ended in stalemate); they succeeded decisively when they rebuilt and maintained the triple alliance (Third War) and combined military action with prior diplomatic isolation (Fourth War).

statement_analysis.statement: The Anglo-Mysore Wars demonstrated that the Subsidiary Alliance System, once deployed, eliminated the possibility of future military resistance from the subjected state, as evidenced by Mysore's complete passivity after 1799.
statement_analysis.reason: The Subsidiary Alliance did not universally eliminate resistance — Mysore was brought under direct British administration in 1831 due to alleged misgovernance (suggesting friction), and across India, several subsidiary states (Awadh, Jhansi) later became centres of the 1857 uprising. 'Completely eliminated future resistance' overstates the system's effectiveness.

statement_analysis.statement: The removal of Tipu Sultan as a significant military power in 1799 was a strategic precondition that enabled the British to direct their full resources toward the Maratha confederacy in the subsequent Anglo-Maratha Wars.
statement_analysis.reason: With Mysore neutralized, the British had a secure southern flank and could concentrate on the Maratha confederacy. The Second Anglo-Maratha War began in 1803, just four years after Seringapatam, confirming the causal sequence.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Selecting '1, 2 and 3' attracts candidates who accept Statement 2's 'complete passivity' claim as a broad characterization of the Subsidiary Alliance's effect, without engaging with the specific counter-evidence (1831 annexation, 1857 uprising patterns).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2: 'Complete passivity' and 'eliminated possibility of future military resistance' is a scope-extension error. Mysore was annexed in 1831 due to friction; subsidiary states elsewhere did rebel in 1857. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 1: The pattern of coalition dynamics determining war outcomes is historically well-supported — Statement 1 is correct.

Verify Statement 3: The Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803) followed Seringapatam (1799) by four years; the causal logic (southern flank secured → northern attention freed) is standard historical analysis — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (a): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses 'completely eliminated' and 'complete passivity' — extreme qualifiers that are never historically accurate. The Subsidiary Alliance was effective in suppressing overt military resistance but did not make subjected states permanently passive. The 1831 annexation of Mysore (due to alleged misgovernance — a form of ongoing British interference suggesting the arrangement was not frictionless) and the 1857 uprising in multiple subsidiary states demonstrate that the system's effects were not absolute. The trap rewards students who think critically about scope-extension qualifiers.
solution.final_explanation:
The comparative analysis of all four Anglo-Mysore Wars is a synthesis question requiring knowledge across the entire arc of the conflict.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The wars' outcomes correlate strongly with coalition management. British defeats/stalemates in Wars 1 and 2 occurred precisely when their coalitions collapsed. British victories in Wars 3 and 4 followed systematic pre-war diplomatic coalition-building. Military technology and manpower were secondary to alliance architecture.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: 'Completely eliminated the possibility of future military resistance' overextends the Subsidiary Alliance's actual effect. Mysore was directly annexed by the British in 1831 due to alleged misgovernance — demonstrating ongoing friction. Elsewhere, subsidiary states including Awadh and Jhansi became epicenters of the 1857 uprising. The system suppressed but did not erase resistance.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The causal connection between Mysore's neutralization (1799) and the focus on the Marathas (Second Anglo-Maratha War, 1803; Third, 1817) is one of the most important structural observations about British expansion in peninsular India. Mysore's fall cleared the southern flank.

Value Addition:
• The 1857 uprising in Awadh (a subsidiary state) is the strongest counter-example to the 'subsidiary alliances prevent resistance' assumption.
• The Anglo-Mysore Wars as a sequence represent the most studied arc of British expansion in UPSC Mains — synthesis across all four wars is a standard essay prompt.
• Coalition management as a British strategic asset: this theme recurs in the Anglo-Maratha Wars and the Anglo-Sikh Wars.

solution.concept_anchor: Mysore 1831 annexation and 1881 restoration — long-arc history
solution.strong_distractor: b — '1857 and 1882' is an attractive distractor because the 1857 rebellion is strongly associated with British annexation policies (Doctrine of Lapse, Awadh annexation) and candidates may incorrectly link Mysore's annexation to that period.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): 1799 is when Mysore was placed under a Subsidiary Alliance with the Wodeyars restored — not directly annexed. 1858 is when the Crown assumed sovereignty after the 1857 Mutiny — neither year matches Mysore's specific annexation/restoration cycle.
Eliminate (b): Mysore was not annexed in 1857 — the 1857 events centered on North India; Mysore had been directly administered since 1831.
Eliminate (c): 1824 and 1875 do not correspond to documented Mysore administrative milestones.
Select (d): Mysore was placed under direct British administration in 1831 (misgovernance pretext) and restored to the Wodeyar dynasty in 1881 under Lord Ripon — the correct years.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The 1831 and 1881 dates for Mysore are precise factual anchors that many candidates do not memorize. The trap exploits the association between the Doctrine of Lapse (1848–1856) and British annexation — candidates who associate annexation with Dalhousie's era may incorrectly place Mysore's annexation in the 1850s. Mysore's 1831 annexation predates Dalhousie by nearly two decades and was based on the misgovernance pretext, not the Doctrine of Lapse.
solution.final_explanation:
The post-1799 administrative history of Mysore has two distinct phases that are independently examinable.

• Option (a): 1799 and 1858 — Incorrect. 1799 is when the Wodeyars were restored under a Subsidiary Alliance, not when Mysore was annexed. 1858 is the year the Crown assumed governance of British India after 1857 — unrelated to Mysore's specific administration cycle.
• Option (b): 1857 and 1882 — Incorrect. Mysore's direct British administration began in 1831, not 1857. The 1882 date is also off by one year from the restoration (1881).
• Option (c): 1824 and 1875 — Incorrect. Neither date corresponds to documented Mysore administrative milestones.
• Option (d): 1831 and 1881 — Correct. The British took direct administrative control of Mysore in 1831 citing alleged misgovernance. In 1881, under the Governor-Generalship of Lord Ripon, Mysore was restored to the Wodeyar dynasty and subsequently became celebrated as a model native state.

Value Addition:
• The misgovernance pretext used for Mysore in 1831 is structurally identical to the one used for Awadh in 1856 — but the outcomes differed dramatically: Mysore was restored; Awadh was never restored.
• Under Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV (20th century), Mysore became one of the most administratively and industrially developed princely states in British India.
• Lord Ripon (1880–1884) is better known for the Ilbert Bill controversy — his restoration of Mysore is a less-discussed but equally significant act of his tenure.

solution.concept_anchor: Battle of Cuddalore 1783 — French victory neutralized by Treaty of Paris

statement_analysis.statement: The Battle of Cuddalore (1783) was a French naval victory over the British East India Company's fleet off the Coromandel Coast and occurred during the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
statement_analysis.reason: The Battle of Cuddalore (June 20, 1783) was fought between the French fleet under Suffren and the British fleet under Admiral Edward Hughes — it was a French victory and did occur during the Second Anglo-Mysore War (1780–1784).

statement_analysis.statement: The strategic gains achieved by France at Cuddalore were subsequently consolidated into a permanent French naval presence in the Bay of Bengal, marking the beginning of sustained French military presence in South India.
statement_analysis.reason: The Treaty of Paris (1783), which ended the American Revolutionary War, required both France and Britain to restore all conquests made in India. Cuddalore's gains were nullified; France established no permanent naval presence in the Bay of Bengal.

solution.strong_distractor: a — 'Both statements correct' is the primary trap because Statement 1 is accurate and Statement 2 sounds like a natural historical consequence — students may accept the 'consolidation of gains' as plausible without knowing that the Treaty of Paris reversed all French gains.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Battle of Cuddalore (June 1783), French fleet under Suffren, victory over British fleet — occurred during the Second Anglo-Mysore War. Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The Treaty of Paris (1783) required mutual restitution of all Indian conquests — French gains at Cuddalore were nullified, not consolidated. No permanent French naval presence followed. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect = option (c).
Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the natural historical narrative: if France won a naval battle, students expect consolidation of that gain. The Treaty of Paris (1783) — which students primarily associate with the end of the American Revolutionary War — had a direct Indian dimension: all French and British conquests in India were to be restored. This Indian clause of the 1783 Paris treaty is a frequently overlooked detail that nullified Cuddalore's significance entirely.
solution.final_explanation:
The Battle of Cuddalore (1783) is one of the most consequential 'what might have been' events in South Indian history — a French naval victory that was diplomatically negated.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Cuddalore (June 20, 1783) was fought between Admiral Suffren's French fleet and Admiral Hughes's British fleet. The French won, making it the most significant French naval action in Indian waters during the Anglo-Mysore Wars.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Treaty of Paris (September 1783) settled the American Revolutionary War and included a provision requiring both France and Britain to restore all conquests made in India since a specific date. This meant Cuddalore's gains could not be held; France established no permanent naval presence. The entire French strategic gain in the Indian theater was negated by the European peace settlement.

Value Addition:
• Admiral Suffren is one of France's most celebrated naval commanders — his Indian Ocean campaign (1781–83) is studied in French naval history as tactically brilliant but strategically futile.
• The 1783 Treaty of Paris is distinct from the 1763 Treaty of Paris — both are Indian history relevant; 1763 ended the Seven Years' War and formalized French exclusion from India.
• The lesson from Cuddalore: military victories in a theater war can be diplomatically reversed by the metropolitan peace — a principle relevant to Mains answers on colonial geopolitics.

solution.concept_anchor: Treaty of Seringapatam 1792 — territorial cessions to three powers
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) swaps Dharwar (Marathas) with Guntur (Nizam), which is the most common territorial attribution error in this treaty.
elimination_logic: Anchor on the clearest pair: Malabar is associated with British commercial interest (pepper, cardamom) — British received Malabar. A-1.
Tipu's sons as hostages: Abdul Khaliq and Muiz-ud-Din were taken to Madras — C with the hostage clause (3).
Dharwar and Raichur are in the northern Deccan/Karnataka — geographically closer to Maratha domains. B-2.
Guntur is in the eastern Deccan, closer to Nizam's territory — D-4. Nizam received Guntur. Correct option: A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4 → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Dharwar-Guntur swap is the primary trap. Both are regional names in the Deccan and both were received by powers allied with the British in the Third War. A student who remembers that the Marathas and Nizam each received territory but cannot precisely recall which territory each received will swap them. Geographic reasoning helps: Dharwar is in present-day northern Karnataka (adjacent to Maratha domains); Guntur is in present-day Andhra Pradesh (adjacent to Nizam's territory).
solution.final_explanation:
The Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) distributed Tipu Sultan's ceded territories among three parties. Precise knowledge of each allocation is testable.

Correct pairings:
• A (Malabar coast) → 1 (British East India Company): Malabar's pepper and cardamom trade was a primary British commercial motivation. Its acquisition gave the Company direct control over the South Asian spice trade.
• B (Dharwar and Raichur districts) → 2 (Maratha Confederacy/Peshwa): These districts in northern Karnataka were the Maratha share of the territorial settlement — geographically contiguous with Maratha domains.
• C (Two sons of Tipu Sultan as hostages) → 3 (Taken to Madras under British custody): Abdul Khaliq and Muiz-ud-Din were taken to Madras. This hostage clause was a personal guarantee of Tipu's compliance with the treaty terms.
• D (Guntur region) → 4 (Nizam of Hyderabad): Guntur, in present-day Andhra Pradesh, was the Nizam's territorial reward — consistent with his eastern geographic position relative to Mysore.

Value Addition:
• Coorg (Kodagu) was also ceded to the British in 1792 — a frequently overlooked fourth British territorial gain from this treaty.
• The financial indemnity of ₹3.3 crore was paid by Tipu to the British alone — allies received territories, not cash.
• Tipu's sons were eventually returned to Mysore after 1799 and treated as pensioners — a relatively humane treatment by British colonial standards.

solution.concept_anchor: Evaluating Tipu's diplomatic outreach — effectiveness vs. romantic portrayal
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is chosen by candidates who admire Tipu's initiative and associate 'pan-Islamic solidarity' with his Ottoman and Afghan outreach, accepting it as a proto-nationalist framework without critically evaluating its actual effectiveness.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): While Tipu did reach out to Ottoman Turkey and Afghanistan, these were pragmatic anti-British diplomatic moves, not expressions of pan-Islamic ideology. Moreover, they produced no effective military alliance — characterizing them as a 'successful pan-Islamic solidarity strategy' is factually incorrect on both ideological and effectiveness grounds.

Eliminate (b): Tipu's outreach to France, Ottoman Turkey, and Afghanistan cannot be characterized as 'successful' — France was preoccupied with the Revolution; Zaman Shah faced Persian pressure; Ottomans were too distant. The alliances never materialized into military cooperation.

Eliminate (d): Tipu's diplomatic outreach was real, not merely symbolic — he sent actual embassies with real correspondence. Describing it as 'entirely symbolic with no material intent' misrepresents the historical record.

Select (c): The outreach was ambitious and genuine in intent, but failed to produce any effective anti-British military coalition due to circumstances external to Mysore — French Revolution, Persian pressure on Afghanistan, Ottoman distance. This is the accurate and nuanced historical assessment.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question tests the UPSC-specific skill of evaluating historical claims critically rather than romanticizing them. Tipu Sultan's diplomatic outreach is often presented in nationalist historiography as heroic proto-nationalist resistance. The examiner tests whether a candidate can simultaneously acknowledge the genuine ambition and initiative of Tipu's diplomacy while recognizing that it produced no effective military alliance. Option (a) glorifies; option (b) overstates success; option (d) denies reality. Only option (c) captures the nuanced historical truth.
solution.final_explanation:
Tipu Sultan's diplomatic outreach is one of the most debated topics in Anglo-Mysore historiography — and a test of analytical sophistication in UPSC Mains.

Scenario analysis:
A ruler sends multiple embassies to different powers over 12 years but receives no material military assistance from any of them, yet the embassies become the pretext his enemy uses to justify a preemptive war. This is precisely Tipu Sultan's situation:

• France: Promised sympathy, sent officers, but no military force. French Revolution and subsequent wars consumed French resources.
• Ottoman Turkey: Too distant; its own conflicts with European powers made Indian intervention impossible.
• Zaman Shah of Afghanistan: Preoccupied with Persia (Qajar dynasty pressure) and internal succession — sent no troops.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The outreach was not a 'pan-Islamic solidarity strategy' — it was a pragmatic anti-British coalition effort. And it did not succeed in building an effective alliance.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The embassies did not succeed in creating an effective military alliance — success would require actual military cooperation.
• Option (c): Correct. Tipu's diplomacy was genuine and sophisticated in design, but external circumstances (French Revolution, Zaman Shah's Persian preoccupation, Ottoman distance) prevented any materialization.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The embassies had real material intent — Tipu was genuinely seeking military allies, not merely making symbolic gestures.

Value Addition:
• Wellesley's use of Tipu's French correspondence as pretext for the Fourth War is a masterclass in how diplomatic contacts can be repackaged as military threats.
• Tipu's 'proto-nationalist' characterization in Indian nationalist historiography (Nehru era) vs. his contested legacy in contemporary historiography is a significant UPSC Mains debate.
• The failure of Tipu's coalition strategy underscores that 18th-century Indian rulers had limited ability to project diplomatic power beyond the subcontinent.

(d) Tipu's foreign policy outreach was entirely symbolic with no material military intent, serving only to enhance his domestic political prestige

solution.concept_anchor: Warren Hastings — Second Anglo-Mysore War strategic context

statement_analysis.statement: Warren Hastings's strategic role during the Second Anglo-Mysore War included authorizing offensive military operations in the Carnatic while simultaneously managing the threat of French naval intervention along the Coromandel Coast.
statement_analysis.reason: Warren Hastings as Governor-General during the Second War (1780–84) did oversee both the land campaign in the Carnatic and the threat of French naval support for Hyder Ali/Tipu — managing these dual pressures was central to his wartime governance.

statement_analysis.statement: Warren Hastings was the Governor-General who personally led the siege of Seringapatam in 1784, forcing Tipu Sultan to accept the terms of the Treaty of Mangalore.
statement_analysis.reason: No siege of Seringapatam occurred in 1784. The Treaty of Mangalore was negotiated without a siege — Tipu and the British reached a mutual restitution agreement. Cornwallis (not Hastings) besieged Seringapatam in 1792 during the Third War.

statement_analysis.statement: Warren Hastings opposed the Treaty of Mangalore, which ended the Second Anglo-Mysore War, believing that the British had not exploited their strategic position sufficiently to impose more favorable terms.
statement_analysis.reason: Hastings publicly opposed the Treaty of Mangalore as a humiliation, arguing that the British were in a strong enough position to demand better terms from Tipu Sultan. The treaty was negotiated by the Madras Council partly without his approval.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Selecting '1 and 3 only' as incorrect (the answer to the NOT correct question) would be wrong; candidates who are uncertain about Statement 2's fabricated siege claim may choose the option that excludes Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 2: No siege of Seringapatam occurred in 1784 — the Treaty of Mangalore was a negotiated mutual restitution, not a surrender after a siege. The 1784 siege attribution to Hastings is a fabrication. Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 1: Hastings managed both Carnatic land operations and French naval threats during the Second War — this is factually accurate. Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Hastings did oppose the Treaty of Mangalore as insufficiently advantageous — this is documented. Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 2 is not correct — option (a): 2 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 fabricates a siege of Seringapatam in 1784 and attributes it to Hastings. Students who know Hastings was the Governor-General during the Second War, and who know Seringapatam was besieged during the Anglo-Mysore Wars, may conflate the 1792 siege (by Cornwallis, Third War) with a non-existent 1784 siege (Hastings, Second War). The precise facts — no siege occurred at Seringapatam in the Second War; the Treaty of Mangalore was a negotiated peace — are the differentiating knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
Warren Hastings's role in the Second Anglo-Mysore War requires distinguishing between what he actually did and what students may incorrectly attribute to him.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Hastings managed the dual challenge of land warfare in the Carnatic and French naval intervention. His coordination of military strategy from Calcutta while dealing with the Battle of Pollilur aftermath (1780) and the Cuddalore naval engagement (1783) was the defining feature of his wartime role.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: There was no siege of Seringapatam in 1784. The Second War ended with the Treaty of Mangalore — a negotiated mutual restitution. Warren Hastings never personally led a siege of Seringapatam. The only Seringapatam siege ending in British victory was in 1792 under Cornwallis (Third War). The final fall came in 1799 under Arthur Wellesley's operational command.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Hastings's opposition to Mangalore is historically documented. He viewed it as a political failure — the British could have extracted better terms. This stance contributed to the broader political context of his eventual impeachment.

Value Addition:
• The Madras Council's independent negotiation of Mangalore (partly bypassing Hastings) reflects the ongoing tension between the Governor-General and Presidency Councils that the Pitt's India Act (1784) was designed to resolve.
• Hastings's impeachment trial (1787–1795) is a landmark in British parliamentary history — Edmund Burke's prosecution is frequently cited in governance contexts.
• The three sieges of Seringapatam: 1792 (Cornwallis — Tipu sued for peace), 1799 (Arthur Wellesley operational command — Tipu killed) — are two distinct events; the first did not end in a storming.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Treaty of Mangalore (1784)' is the most dangerous distractor because it also contained mutual restitution provisions and is similarly 'equal' — candidates who know 'equal treaty' but not which war it ended may confuse the two.
elimination_logic: The blank requires a treaty that (1) ended the First Anglo-Mysore War, (2) included a defensive alliance clause, and (3) was subsequently violated when the British refused to aid Hyder Ali in 1771.
Eliminate (b): The Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) ended the Third War with punitive terms — no defensive alliance clause.
Eliminate (c): The Treaty of Mangalore (1784) ended the Second War — by 1771 (when the Maratha invasion occurred), this treaty did not yet exist.
Eliminate (d): The Treaty of Salbai (1782) ended the First Anglo-Maratha War — entirely different conflict and time period.
Select (a): The Treaty of Madras (1769) ended the First Anglo-Mysore War, included a defensive alliance clause, and was violated by British inaction during the 1771 Maratha invasion of Mysore.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The primary trap is the Treaty of Mangalore, which shares the 'equal treaty / mutual restitution' characterization with the Treaty of Madras. A candidate who knows the defensive alliance clause was broken but anchors this to the wrong treaty will choose Mangalore. The temporal key: the British violated a treaty provision in 1771, meaning the treaty must have been signed before 1771 — only the Treaty of Madras (1769) qualifies. Mangalore was signed in 1784.
solution.final_explanation:
The defensive alliance clause of the Treaty of Madras is one of the most consequential provisions in Anglo-Mysore diplomatic history — its violation directly caused the Second War.

• Option (a): Treaty of Madras (1769) — Correct. This treaty ended the First War and included a mutual defensive alliance clause requiring each party to aid the other if attacked by a third power. When the Marathas invaded Mysore in 1771, Hyder Ali invoked this clause. British inaction constituted a direct breach and radicalized Hyder Ali's hostility toward the British.
• Option (b): Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) — Incorrect. This punitive treaty ended the Third War. It contained no defensive alliance clause — it imposed territorial cessions, financial indemnity, and hostages.
• Option (c): Treaty of Mangalore (1784) — Incorrect. While also on broadly equal terms, it was signed in 1784 — thirteen years after the 1771 Maratha invasion. It cannot be the treaty violated in 1771.
• Option (d): Treaty of Salbai (1782) — Incorrect. This treaty ended the First Anglo-Maratha War and has no connection to Mysore's defensive alliance history.

Value Addition:
• The 1771 Maratha invasion of Mysore (against which the British declined to act) is historically cited as the immediate cause of Hyder Ali's decision to seek alliances against the British.
• The defensive alliance clause of 1769 is structurally similar to Article V of NATO (collective defence) — a useful conceptual parallel for Mains answers.
• The British breach of 1771 was not formally acknowledged — the Second War was fought without any British admission of treaty violation.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Selecting (a) is the trap for candidates who uncritically accept nationalist historiography: both A and R seem true, and the 'freedom fighter' framing appears to explain the 'Tiger of Mysore' symbolism, making the causal link feel natural.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — Tipu Sultan's legacy is genuinely contested in Indian historiography — from freedom fighter (nationalist school) to complex figure (contemporary revisionist scholarship touching on his religious policies and administrative record). A is correct.

Step 2: Is R correct? — The 'Tiger of Mysore' epithet is historically associated with Tipu Sultan's personal symbolism (tiger motifs on weapons, throne, and uniforms). R is correct as a factual claim about the epithet.

Step 3: Does R explain A? — The 'Tiger of Mysore' symbolism (a personal style choice in court aesthetics) does not cause or explain the historiographical controversy about his legacy. The controversy stems from debates about his religious policies toward non-Muslims, his administrative record, and whether his resistance qualifies as proto-nationalism. R is a decorative fact unrelated to why the historiography is contested. R does NOT explain A.
Both A and R correct, R does not explain A — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: This question targets candidates who accept the 'nationalist hero' framing of Tipu without critical analysis. The assertion (A) about contested historiography is factually correct — Tipu's legacy is debated. The reason (R) about the 'Tiger of Mysore' symbolism is also factually correct. But the reason has no causal relationship to why the historiography is contested. The controversy arises from evidence about his treatment of religious minorities (including Coorgis, Mangalorean Catholics, and some Hindus) and questions about whether his resistance can be characterized as 'nationalist' in the modern sense — none of which is caused by or related to the tiger symbolism.
solution.final_explanation:
Tipu Sultan's historical legacy is one of the most genuinely contested topics in Indian history and a sophisticated UPSC Mains test of multi-perspective analysis.

Assertion (A): Correct. Tipu Sultan's legacy is not settled — nationalist historians from Jawaharlal Nehru onward have celebrated him as a freedom fighter; contemporary scholarship has raised questions about his religious policies toward Coorgis, Mangalorean Catholics, and some Hindu communities, while others defend the evidence as exaggerated or misrepresented. The historiographical debate is real.

Reason (R): Correct. The 'Tiger of Mysore' epithet is historically grounded — tiger motifs appeared on Tipu's throne, weapons, and military uniforms. The symbolism represented ferocity and was central to his self-presentation.

Causal relationship: R does not explain A. The controversy over Tipu's legacy arises from debates about his administrative and religious conduct — not from his court symbolism. A candidate must ask: does the tiger symbolism cause the historiographical debate? No — the debate stems from evidence about his treatment of non-Muslims and questions about proto-nationalism. R is factually true but causally unrelated to A.

Value Addition:
• UPSC Mains questions on Tipu require presenting multiple perspectives without accepting or rejecting either hagiographic or vilifying accounts.
• The Government of India's postage stamp honoring Tipu Sultan (1974) represents the nationalist reading; subsequent controversies in Karnataka represent the revisionist challenge.
• Tipu's personal library, captured in 1799, is partly held in the British Library — a cultural heritage dimension sometimes tested in Art and Culture questions.

solution.concept_anchor: Comparative features of Anglo-Mysore War outcomes — precise attributions

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Madras (1769) is unique among Anglo-Mysore settlements in being the only agreement where the British were compelled to accept terms that were disadvantageous to them, including a defensive alliance clause.
statement_analysis.reason: The Treaty of Madras stands apart: it was signed under duress (Hyder Ali's march on Madras), required the British to accept mutual terms including a defensive alliance, and is historically recognized as the most humiliating settlement the British signed in the Anglo-Mysore conflicts.

statement_analysis.statement: The Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) required Tipu Sultan to pay a financial indemnity of ₹3.3 crore to the British and cede territories to all three allied powers — British, Marathas, and Nizam — while also providing two sons as hostages.
statement_analysis.reason: All three elements are accurate: the ₹3.3 crore indemnity to the British; territorial cessions to British (Malabar, Coorg, Baramahal), Marathas (Dharwar, Raichur), and Nizam (Guntur); and the hostage clause (Abdul Khaliq and Muiz-ud-Din taken to Madras).

statement_analysis.statement: The Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799) concluded with a formal treaty between the British and the restored Wodeyar dynasty, establishing the terms of the Subsidiary Alliance.
statement_analysis.reason: The Fourth War did not conclude with a formal treaty — it ended with Tipu's death and the fall of Seringapatam. The Wodeyar restoration and Subsidiary Alliance arrangements were administrative decisions made post-conflict, not a formal peace treaty concluded between warring parties.

statement_analysis.statement: Warren Hastings's opposition to the Treaty of Mangalore stemmed from his belief that the British military position at the time warranted more punitive terms against Tipu Sultan.
statement_analysis.reason: Hastings believed the British had sufficient military and strategic advantage after the Second War to impose better terms; his opposition to Mangalore was based on this assessment of missed strategic opportunity, not on abstract principles.

solution.strong_distractor: d — 'All four' is the trap for candidates who accept Statement 3's 'formal treaty' claim without precisely recalling that the Fourth War ended with Tipu's death rather than a negotiated settlement.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 3 carefully: the Fourth War ended with Tipu's death on May 4, 1799 — there was no formal peace treaty. The Wodeyar restoration and Subsidiary Alliance were post-conflict arrangements, not treaty terms negotiated between belligerents. Statement 3 is incorrect.

Verify Statements 1, 2, and 4: Treaty of Madras being uniquely humiliating to the British is correct; all three specific terms of Seringapatam (1792) are accurate; Hastings's opposition to Mangalore on strategic opportunity grounds is documented.
Three statements correct (1, 2, 4), one incorrect (3) — 'Only three.'
Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 contains a plausible-but-false element: 'a formal treaty between the British and the restored Wodeyar dynasty.' Students who know the Subsidiary Alliance was established after 1799 may assume it was formalized as a treaty at the war's conclusion. The critical distinction: the Fourth War ended with Tipu's death, not with a negotiated peace treaty. The post-war arrangements (restoration, Subsidiary Alliance) were imposed administrative decisions, not bilaterally negotiated treaty terms.
solution.final_explanation:
This synthesis question tests precise knowledge of all four Anglo-Mysore War outcomes simultaneously.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Treaty of Madras (1769) is the only agreement in the entire series where the British negotiated under compulsion. Hyder Ali's march on Madras created the pressure; the defensive alliance clause was uniquely humiliating.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) contains three independently testable provisions: ₹3.3 crore indemnity (to British only); territorial tripartite cession (British — Malabar/Coorg/Baramahal; Marathas — Dharwar/Raichur; Nizam — Guntur); hostage clause (Abdul Khaliq and Muiz-ud-Din).
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Fourth War had no formal peace treaty. Tipu died fighting on May 4, 1799. Post-conflict arrangements were imposed by the British unilaterally — the Wodeyar restoration and Subsidiary Alliance were not negotiated treaty terms.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Hastings's opposition to Mangalore was strategic: he believed the British military position (despite the stalemate of the Second War) was strong enough to demand punitive terms. His opposition reflects the 'forward policy' instinct that characterized his entire tenure.

Value Addition:
• The absence of a formal treaty ending the Fourth War distinguishes it from all other major Anglo-Indian conflicts of the era.
• The three separately verifiable clauses of the Treaty of Seringapatam (1792) are a standard Prelims fact-cluster.
• Across the four wars: Treaty of Madras → Treaty of Mangalore → Treaty of Seringapatam → No treaty. The progressive reduction in Mysore's negotiating power is encapsulated in this sequence.
